genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the man described builds pipe instruments
he picks out dried wood without flaws
he melts a metal mixture into thin sheets
these sheets are rolled to form the pipes
the pressure of the bellows must be adjusted
too much pressure gives a harsh tone
too little pressure weakens the tone
tuning slightly alters the length of the pipes
he stops working when his hearing tires
text: An organ builder works slowly, and every motion he makes answers to a measurement. Wood comes first. He picks out boards that have dried for years, throws aside any board with a knot in it, and planes them down until the thickness holds steady from one end to the other. Metal comes second. He melts tin and lead together, pours the alloy out into thin sheets, and rolls each sheet into a pipe that speaks the moment air crosses it. Air comes third. He sets the pressure of the bellows with care, because too strong a wind turns the note shrill, while too weak a wind smothers it altogether. Tuning comes last, and it is the hardest part of the whole trade. He shaves or draws out each pipe by a hair, until the high voice stops beating against the low one. His ears give out long before his hands, he says, and that is the moment he puts the tools down.

units: the evening opened with a short piece for low strings
the first sound filled the space without excess
a lone singer then performed a work with restraint
the writer points out how young this performer is
the second half of the program convinced less
the brass instruments buried the wooden wind instruments
a string instrument out of tune made an unpleasant noise
the conductor flagged the mishap with a single look
the last chord hung under the ceiling of the hall
the writer judges this group uneven against its ambitions
text: The evening opened with a short piece for low strings alone, and their thick sound filled the hall without ever crowding it. A singer followed, unaccompanied, shaping every phrase with a restraint you seldom hear from a performer that young. The second half of the program went less well. The brass sat too far forward and buried the woodwinds, so the middle of the texture simply went missing. One violin had slipped out of tune, and a brief scrape cut across the room, which the conductor put right with a single look. The closing section drew every desk together at last, and the final chord hung under the vaulted ceiling for what felt like a suspended stretch of time. You come away with the impression of an uneven group, superb once it stops chasing effect, shaky the moment it reaches for sheer power.

units: the writer is writing from a rehearsal room
the room has no heat and the air is damp
the damp warps the wood and slackens the strings
the instrument loses its tuning after half an hour
the retuning eats up half of the session
the leader has seen the same trouble on his bow
his request for a heating unit was turned down
the group falls back on a tighter room next door
the bare walls of that room swell the low sounds
the writer asks the reader to bring a tuning fork
text: I am writing from the room where we rehearse, since I got here well ahead of everyone else. The place has no heat at all, and the damp cold works away at my instrument. The wood shrinks, the strings go slack, and the tuning falls apart after half an hour. Retuning eats up half the session, which wears the rest of the group down as well. Our leader finally worked out why, once his own bow had begun rasping in the same way. He asked for a portable heater and was turned down flat. So we squeeze into the room next door, which is tighter, with bare walls that throw the sound straight back and set the low notes humming. I will take that over the cold. If you come by at the end of the week, bring your tuning fork. Mine has rung false ever since I dropped it, and I no longer dare trust it.

units: a sound professional is asked about her hearing health
she blames the wear on quiet drawn out mixing sessions
listening at low volume forces sustained attention
she gave up on the ear protection she had bought
that protection skewed how she heard the high frequencies
she breaks off her listening at regular intervals
she holds herself to a volume ceiling she never crosses
she sometimes turns down a session when she feels drained
the ringing in the evening has dropped off sharply
text: What is it that wears down the hearing of a sound engineer fastest? She answers without pausing at all. Not concerts, she says, but the long quiet mixing sessions that stretch on for hours, where the ear strains at low volume to catch the smallest details. And the remedy? She bought earplugs first, then let them sit unused in a drawer, because they smother the high frequencies and skew her judgment. What she does now rests on three habits. She kills the sound at regular intervals so that her ears can rest for a while. She holds herself to a ceiling she never crosses, however hard a client pushes her. The third habit is the hardest of all, and it means turning a session down whenever she feels her hearing giving out. Since then, she says, the ringing that used to fill her head at night has all but stopped.

units: two professionals judge the same place differently
the man finds the sound of the stage too flat
he blames the drapes for soaking up the high frequencies
the singer feels held up there by her returning voice
the side walls send her own singing back to her
both of them notice that the floor shakes with low sounds
that shaking throws off the readings of the technician
it works as a rhythmic marker for the singer
she hums under her breath in the other place for reassurance
the technician prefers a place that adds no color
text: The technician and the singer do not describe the same hall at all. He finds the stage flat and dull to his ear, and he blames the heavy drapes, which soak up the highs and hand him back something soft and shapeless. She feels held up there instead, since her own voice comes back to her off the side walls. On one point, at least, the two of them agree. The floor shakes as soon as the low notes begin to rise. He calls that a flaw, because the tremor blurs the readings he takes. She calls it a support, because she feels the beat under her feet before she hears it at all. Asked about the wider hall next door, she admits that she hums under her breath there just to reassure herself, the silence feels so hollow. He much prefers that one. A room that adds nothing, he says, finally lets you hear what is being played.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the writer traces early music back to three motions of the hand
the first motion is to strike
a skin stretched over a hollow box gives a low carrying sound
the second motion rests on breathing
a hollow plant stalk with holes turns breath into a note
closing or opening the holes shifts the pitch
the third motion is to pluck
a tight string let go gives a short lived sound
a cavity was added to draw out the vibration
these three beginnings still show in the shape of instruments
text: All early music comes down to three motions that the hands learned apart from one another. The first of them is the strike. A skin stretched over a hollow frame answers the blow and shakes the air around it, which is where drums come from, and their rumble carries farther than any voice. The second is the breath. A hollow stalk, bored through with uneven holes, turns plain air into a note, and fingers that close or free the holes push the pitch up or down. The third is the pluck. A string drawn tight between two fixed points sounds only briefly when you pull it aside and let it go. A hollow box was soon added underneath, so that the shaking would last longer and grow louder. The three families later mixed together, yet their beginnings can still be read in the shape of the instruments.

units: a string pulled aside swings around its resting place
that swinging squeezes then frees the air beside it
the disturbance travels along from one point to the next
the air particles themselves barely move
the outer ear guides the wave toward a canal
a thin membrane starts swinging at the end of that canal
three small bones strengthen that motion
a coiled organ full of fluid then takes in the vibration
cells topped with hairs turn the motion into nerve signals
the rate of the swings sets the pitch that is heard
text: A plucked string leaves its resting place behind, comes back to it, then overshoots it once again. That back and forth is what we call vibration. It squeezes the air molecules beside it, which bunch up and then spread out in turn, passing the shove along to the ones beyond them. The wave travels outward that way, step by step, while the air itself barely moves at all. The outer ear funnels it into a narrow canal, and at the far end of it a thin membrane starts swinging at the very same rate. Three tiny bones pick up that motion, strengthen it, and hand it on to a coiled organ that is full of fluid. Inside, cells topped with fine hairs bend over and fire off a nerve signal. The nerve carries that signal to the brain, which hears a high or a low note depending on how fast the swings arrive.

units: a flaw in the casting had cracked a bell
the crack could not be seen without examination
it split the vibration into two parts out of tune
the ringing gave a beating instead of a clean sound
neighbors complained without grasping where the noise came from
the local assembly had the bell taken down
a specialist declared the repair impossible
she explained that welding changes the density of the metal
the bell was cast again with its own alloy
putting it back in service stopped walkers in their tracks
text: A flaw in the casting, invisible to the naked eye, had cracked the bell up in the tower. The split ran under the lip of the bronze and broke the vibration into two parts that no longer agreed with each other. Every peal gave a dull beating instead of the full tone people expected, and neighbors complained about a grating ring without ever knowing where it came from. The local assembly voted to take the bell down, a long and costly job. A founder was called in, and she ruled out any repair at all. Welded metal no longer holds the same density, she said, and the tone suffers for it. She offered instead to melt the whole thing down again with its own bronze. The recast bell went back up as the cold season ended, and its first peal rang so cleanly that walkers stopped where they stood.

units: the text speaks to whoever plays in an overly echoing room
the notes pile up and blur the fast passages
the stiff surfaces send the sound back without taking it in
a clap of the hands serves to gauge how long the tail lasts
a rug on the floor treats the bounce between floor and ceiling
a thick cloth is hung on one wall only
covering every wall would leave the room lifeless
shifting the music stand to an angle keeps low sounds from building
a second clap lets you check the result
text: You practice in a room where every note drags on behind the next one, and fast passages turn to mush. Hard surfaces are the cause, since they send the sound straight back at you instead of taking it in. Work through this in order. Clap once in the middle of the room and listen to the tail. The longer it hangs on, the more correction you are going to need. Lay a thick rug on the floor first, because the bounce between floor and ceiling is the most stubborn one of all. Hang a heavy blanket on the wall your instrument faces, and on that wall only. Cover all four and the room goes lifeless, with the highs swallowed. Then swing the music stand to an angle, because a square placement builds up the low notes and sets them droning. Clap again. If the tail has come down by half, stop right there.

units: a student survey compares two neighboring urban areas
the workshop area puts up with steady machine noise
that constant noise ends up slipping past the attention of residents
the area of the wide streets shows a lower average level
abrupt traffic sounds break out there without warning
it is those sudden peaks that cut into rest
one resident sets the steady hum against the biting sound
the survey also covered the nighttime hours
night deliveries bring on ringing ears and exhaustion
the authors conclude that the unexpected tires more than the intensity
text: Two neighboring districts live with noise in opposite ways, and a student survey has just borne that out. On the workshop side, the machines never stop, but their drone is steady, and residents say they grow so used to it that they stop hearing it at all. On the avenue side, the average level is lower. It is the horns and the squealing brakes that come out of nowhere, and those short spikes are what pull people out of their rest. One resident put it plainly. A steady hum you end up forgetting, a sound that stings, never. The students also looked at the nights. Where the activity stops, sleep repairs itself. Where deliveries run through, people report ringing ears and heavy exhaustion. Their conclusion fits into a single sentence: it is not the volume that wears you out, it is the surprise.
